references.text: Gershon is mentioned again as Moses' son, and the name is explained by the fact that Moses was a stranger in a foreign land.
Abraham describes himself as a stranger and sojourner, the same theme of being a 'ger' (stranger) in a foreign land.
God tells Abraham that his descendants will be strangers in a land that is not theirs, a prophecy about Israel's stay in Egypt.
Israel is reminded to love the stranger because they themselves were strangers in Egypt, the same theme of being a stranger.
David confesses that they are strangers and guests before God, similar language about being a stranger.
The psalmist describes himself as a stranger and guest with God; the same Hebrew word 'ger' is used.
The psalmist calls himself a stranger on earth, thematically parallel to Moses' experience of being a stranger.
Hebrews mentions people of faith who confessed that they were strangers and foreigners on earth, including Moses' experience.
Peter calls believers strangers and foreigners, the same concept of being a 'ger' in the world.
